title: The Game Changer: Non-Linear Transformations Complete Nash's Agencies Method
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Game Changer: Non-Linear Transformations Complete Nash's Agencies Method
detail.abstract: Nash's agencies method for coalition formation suffers from a critical computational flaw: negative acceptance probabilities when coalition values are large relative to the rationality parameter. This breakdown has prevented practical implementation for over fifteen years. We resolve this instability by replacing linear utility calculations with squared payoffs, ensuring mathematical positivity while preserving the method's core game-theoretic properties. Our approach guarantees 0 < a ij < 1 for all parameter values, enables convergent iterative dynamics, and maintains computational complexity of O(n 3) per iteration. Empirical validation across multiple scenarios, player numbers, and coalition structures confirms stability where the original method fails in 23% of realistic parameter combinations. The squared transformation incurs modest welfare costs (0.6-3.2%) but provides complete algorithmic reliability. This represents a practical solution that completes Nash's unfinished algorithmic framework for coalition formation.

title: Inequalities in the Longevity of Females and Males Aged 65 In Spain, 2008-2021. The Role of Pension Income
affiliations: University of Valencia - Department of Financial Economics, University of Valencia - Faculty of Economics, University of the Basque Country - Department of Applied Economics III (Econometrics and Statistics) and University of Valencia - Department of Financial Economics

detail.title: Inequalities in the Longevity of Females and Males Aged 65 In Spain, 2008-2021. The Role of Pension Income
detail.abstract: Studies using pensions and/or pensionable income as proxies for life expectancy are few and far between. This paper looks at Spain, a country for which until recently very little was known about the life expectancy of pensioners by pension income (PI) level. We use a large administrative data set to estimate inequalities in longevity among pensioners grouped according to their PI levels. We present the results for mortality trends among retirement pensioners aged 65 and over for nine rolling windows covering six years each for the period 2008-2021. We find that life expectancy by PI level at ages 65 (LE65) has a positive link with the PI level for both males and females, and this is true for all the periods analysed. The absolute differences in LE65 between pensioners in the highest and the lowest PI groups fluctuate across the nine rolling windows examined. For males, the differences increase from the beginning (2.67 years) until 4.06 years and then tend to decrease (2.83 years). For females there are also fluctuations (between 1.84 and 2.67 years), but the absolute differences are always smaller than those observed for males. Another finding is that socioeconomic inequality in longevity by PI group is lower when measured with M65 than LE65. We also find that the pensioner population seems to have been more affected by the COVID-19 pandemic than the general population and that two groups of pensionersthe lowest PI group of males and the highest PI group of femalesappear to have improved their longevity during the pandemic.

title: Exploring the Relationship between Classroom Arrangement and Students’ Performance in Cambodian Higher Education: The Role of Self-Regulation
affiliations: Lincoln University College Malaysia and Lincoln University College

detail.title: Exploring the Relationship between Classroom Arrangement and Students’ Performance in Cambodian Higher Education: The Role of Self-Regulation
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of classroom arrangement on students’ academic performance in Cambodian higher education, with a particular focus on the mediating role of self-regulation. A quantitative research design was employed, involving 320 university lecturers who responded to a structured questionnaire. Data analysis was conducted using SmartPLS (PLS-SEM) software. The structural model explains 16.4% of the variance in self-regulation and 15.6% in students' performance, with adjusted R² values of 0.161 and 0.151, indicating acceptable model robustness. Effect size analysis showed that classroom arrangement has a moderate effect on self-regulation (f² = 0.196), a small direct effect on students’ performance (f² = 0.053), and self-regulation has a small positive effect on students' performance (f² = 0.057). The model demonstrated predictive relevance (Q² > 0), supporting its utility. The structural results confirmed that classroom arrangement significantly influences self-regulation (β = 0.408, t = 8.677, p = 0.000) and students’ performance (β = 0.234, t = 3.850, p = 0.000). Self-regulation also positively affects students’ performance (β = 0.242, t = 4.018, p = 0.000) and significantly mediates the relationship between classroom arrangement and students’ performance (β = 0.099, t = 3.487, p = 0.001). These findings highlight the crucial role of classroom environment and self-regulatory behavior in fostering students’ academic success.

Spanish Abstract: La regulación de fusiones y adquisiciones es una de las materias más discutidas dentro del derecho societario, pues supone balancear los intereses dispares de inversores y administradores de la sociedad, producto de la separación entre la propiedad y el control, característica de las empresas cotizadas. Este artículo abordará, en primer lugar y de manera introductoria, algunos aspectos históricos y económicos clave de las operaciones y fusiones que permitirán poner en contexto la regulación tanto española como europea de las Ofertas Públicas de Adquisición. Una vez explicados estos conceptos, el artículo buscará detallar la regulación española de la materia. Así, se examinará escrupulosamente la normativa nacional respecto de todos aquellos ámbitos relacionados con el desarrollo de la OPA.

English Abstract: The regulation of mergers and acquisitions is one of the most debated areas of corporate law, as it involves balancing the disparate interests of investors and company directors, resulting from the separation of ownership and control, characteristic of listed companies. This article will first and foremost address, as an introduction, some key historical and economic aspects of transactions and mergers, which will provide context for both Spanish and European regulations on takeover bids. Once these concepts have been explained, the article will seek to detail the Spanish regulations on this matter. Thus, it will scrupulously examine national regulations regarding all areas related to the conduct of takeover bids.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This paper investigates the causal effect of retirement on grip strength using crosscountry panel data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Design/methodology/approach-We employ a fixed effects instrumental variable (FE-IV) approach, utilising eligibility for state pension age as our instrument. Findings-The findings indicate that retirement enhances grip strength among elderly women but not men. However, increased time spent in retirement reduces grip strength for both men and women. Additionally, our analysis reveals that transitioning to retirement positively impacts elderly adults in individualistic societies, whereas prolonged retirement negatively affects those in collectivistic cultures.

title: AI-Driven Transformation in Banking: From Fraud Detection to Personalized Services
affiliations: Ally Financial (Ally Financial Inc.)

detail.title: AI-Driven Transformation in Banking: From Fraud Detection to Personalized Services
detail.abstract: This paper explores the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the banking sector, focusing on fraud detection, risk assessment, customer service automation, and personalized financial services. We review machine learning (ML) techniques such as supervised learning, anomaly detection, and natural language processing (NLP) implemented in modern banking systems. Case studies from leading banks demonstrate AI's efficacy in reducing fraud losses by 30-40%, improving credit scoring accuracy, and enhancing customer satisfaction through chatbots. Challenges such as data privacy, model interpretability, and regulatory compliance are discussed, along with future directions for explainable AI (XAI) and quantum machine learning in finance.

title: Tariff Smart Beta Strategy: Portfolio Construction under U.S. Tariff Escalations
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Tariff Smart Beta Strategy: Portfolio Construction under U.S. Tariff Escalations
detail.abstract: This paper develops and tests a novel Tariff Smart Beta Strategy that integrates trade policy shocks into systematic portfolio construction. Using U.S. sector-level exchangetraded fund (ETF) data from July 2018 to 2025, coinciding with tariff escalation phases under both Trump administrations, we estimate sectoral tariff betas and examine five portfolio allocation methodologies: (1) inverse beta weighting (1/|β|), (2) β-neutral optimization, (3) equal risk contribution, (4) minimum variance, and (5) maximum Sharpe ratio. Our empirical results show that tariff shocks significantly alter sectoral performance, with technology and consumer discretionary sectors bearing negative tariff betas, while utilities and financials display relative defensiveness. Backtests demonstrate that strategies emphasizing β-neutrality and risk-balanced allocations outperform naive sector benchmarks during tariff escalation periods. The findings contribute to the literature on trade policy uncertainty and factor investing by offering a framework for integrating tariff shocks into smart beta design.

title: The Editor's Problem
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: The Editor's Problem
detail.abstract: An editor maximizing quality  relies on the qualitative recommendation of a reviewer. The reviewer may be biased to accept or reject independently of quality. Using the minimum principle, an averaging rule is found to best reduce the noise introduced by bias: under this rule, an unbiased reviewer accepts when quality is greater than the average quality selected by the editor. For distributions with heavy tails, the probability of acceptance due to bias is bounded away from zero even if almost all reviewers are unbiased. Standards adopted by the editor may be excessive relative to the social optimum. Environments with multiple reviewers,  reviewer histories, detailed reviews and competition between editors do not solve the problem and may worsen it. A dynamic peer review demonstrates the inherent fragility of equilibria with informative reviews. The model applies to many settings, including grant review, evidence selection, medical testing, juries and project selection.

title: Global Working Hours
affiliations: World Bank and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Global Working Hours
detail.abstract:
This paper uses labor force surveys from 160 countries to build a new microdatabase on hours worked covering 97% of the world population in cross section. We also construct time series spanning over 20 years in 86 countries. Hours worked per adult are slightly bell-shaped with GDP per capita but weakly correlated with development overall. Hours worked by the young (aged 15-19) and elderly (aged 60+) decline with development, driven by growing school attendance and public pension coverage. Hours worked among prime-age adults (aged 20-59) are mildly bell-shaped with development for men while they are increasing for women. The fall in male hours in middle-to-higher income countries is driven by reduced hours per worker and is offset by increases in female labor force participation. These two forces have exactly compensated each other in many countries, leading to a remarkable long-run stability of prime-age hours worked. Labor taxes are strongly negatively correlated with prime-age hours worked both in international comparisons and overtime within countries. Controlling for government transfers only partly reduces the link between labor taxes and prime-age hours, ruling out substitution and income effects on labor supply as the only driver. Controlling for working hours regulations and the size of the formal sector eliminates this link, suggesting that regulations also play a large role in reducing intensive hours in higher-income countries.

title: CRS and the Digital Economy: Why Transparency Fails without Enforcement
affiliations: Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE), University of Toronto

detail.title: CRS and the Digital Economy: Why Transparency Fails without Enforcement
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the limits of the OECD's Common Reporting Standard (CRS) in addressing tax avoidance within the digital economy. Unlike FATCA, which enforces compliance through sanctions, CRS depends on voluntary reciprocity and weak oversight, leaving major gaps. Digital platforms such as Amazon, TikTok, and Airbnb illustrate how cross-border financial flows escape effective monitoring. Conflicts with privacy protections, especially under Article 26 of the OECD Model Convention and EU data law, further reduce effectiveness. The argument is simple: transparency without enforcement sustains asymmetry and undermines trust in tax fairness.

title: A System Dynamics Approach to Quantifying the Cost-Effectiveness of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Control on Cattle Production Systems in Rwanda
affiliations: Oklahoma State University, Oklahoma State University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, , International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and Oklahoma State University

detail.title: A System Dynamics Approach to Quantifying the Cost-Effectiveness of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Control on Cattle Production Systems in Rwanda
detail.abstract: CONTEXTFoot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) is an endemic viral disease that disrupts livestock production systems in Rwanda and other sub-Saharan African countries. Livestock systems are interdependent. Cattle population dynamics, production outputs, and economic outcomes are all influenced by disease shocks and control interventions. Understanding the system-wide impacts of FMD and the effectiveness of control strategies requires an integrative modeling approach.OBJECTIVEThis study assesses the long-term impacts of FMD outbreaks on cattle production and the cost-effectiveness of three control strategies: vaccination, quarantine, and a combination of both strategies, using a system-level perspective. METHODSA linked Herd Dynamics Model (HDM) and Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) epidemiological model (Rw-FMD) was used to simulate the interactions and feedback between cattle population dynamics, disease spread, and economic outcomes on a weekly basis through 2035. The model captures system-level processes, including births, natural and disease-induced mortality, and intervention effects. Costs of interventions were incorporated into a system-wide benefit-cost framework to assess the relative economic efficiency of control strategies. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONSSimulations showed that FMD significantly reduces cattle populations, productivity, and economic returns. In the absence of interventions, the cattle population grew to only 1.53 million heads by 2035, compared to 1.96 million in the “combined” scenario. Meat production dropped by 20%, resulting in an economic loss of 761 billion Rwandan francs (RWF). Milk production was 18% lower in the “no control” scenario compared to the “combined” scenario. Among the intervention strategies, vaccination and the combined vaccination-quarantine approach were the most effective in controlling disease spread. However, when considering implementation costs, the quarantine strategy showed the highest benefit-cost ratio (46.34).SIGNIFICANCEBy integrating herd dynamics, epidemiological processes, and economic outcomes, this study provides a system-level understanding of FMD impacts and control strategies. The findings offer guidance for resource allocation and strategic planning in Rwanda, but is applicable to other FMD-affected countries, with the emphasis that cost-effective livestock production systems require both epidemiological and economic considerations.

title: The Effect of Drawdowns on Investment Manager Performance
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: The Effect of Drawdowns on Investment Manager Performance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper No. 5462555
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Drawdowns, defined as peak-to-trough declines in portfolio value, are critical events in investment management that can influence manager performance, investor behavior, and fund flows. This paper examines the impact of drawdowns on investment manager performance across various asset classes, focusing on both short-term and long-term effects, with a focus on historical case studies. While conventional metrics such as volatility, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown are widely used in performance evaluation, the dynamic effects of drawdowns on manager behavior, risk-taking, and subsequent returns remain underexplored. We argue that drawdowns exert asymmetric psychological and financial pressures on managers, influencing portfolio construction, risk appetite, and career trajectories. Our findings indicate that severe drawdowns lead to reduced risk-taking, lower alpha generation, and increased manager turnover, particularly in high-volatility environments. However, managers with strong risk management frameworks exhibit resilience, recovering performance more quickly. The study highlights the interplay between drawdowns, behavioral biases, and performance metrics, offering implications for portfolio managers and investors.

title: Illegal Drug use and Government Policy: Evidence from a Darknet Marketplace
affiliations: Northwestern University - Pritzker School of Law, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance, Uber Technologies Inc. and National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow)

detail.title: Illegal Drug use and Government Policy: Evidence from a Darknet Marketplace
detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural model of demand for illegal drug varieties and studies how consumers substitute between different types of drugs in response to government policies. We use a unique longitudinal dataset on prices, quantities, and individual decisions that we obtained by scraping a darknet marketplace that covered the majority of the retail illegal drug trade in Russia. Our estimation procedure exploits a novel set of micro-level moment conditions to identify correlations in preferences for specific drug types and the degree of attachment to them. We find that the median own-price elasticity of demand for illegal drugs is -3.6, and there is high substitution within two classes of drugs: medium-risk stimulants and cannabis. We validate our estimates using exogenous variation in the price of hashish caused by increased policing. The estimated model is used to evaluate counterfactual drug policies. We find that the legalization of cannabis has the benefit of decreasing the use of riskier drugs while increasing cannabis use. For every 4 additional doses of cannabis consumed, 1 less dose of another drug is consumed. Our estimates show that the recent introduction of a new family of synthetic drugs has increased total drug demand in the country by 40%, suggesting that governments should allocate resources to prevent the introduction of new drug products. Finally, our model helps identify the optimal drugs to target for interdiction, specifically those without close substitutes, such as α-PVP.

title: Calgary Cyclelogistics: Unlocking the Potential for Cargo Bike Delivery
affiliations: Pembina Institute for Appropriate Development, The Pembina Institute and Pembina Institute for Appropriate Development

detail.title: Calgary Cyclelogistics: Unlocking the Potential for Cargo Bike Delivery
detail.abstract: Freight traffic is increasing in cities across Canada, driven in part by the rise of online shopping. As more delivery trucks and vans travel through metropolitan areas, they contribute to air and noise pollution, traffic congestion and greenhouse gas emissions, and can pose safety risks to other road users. To improve the efficiency and sustainability of urban goods movement, cities and businesses are exploring alternatives such as the delivery of goods by bike. This approach, often referred to as “cyclelogistics,” includes the use of pedal-powered or electric-assist bicycles, tricycles and other multi-wheeled cycles. This report examines the potential for cyclelogistics in the City of Calgary. Drawing on research, interviews and lessons from other jurisdictions, it identifies strategies the City can use to enable and expand cargo bike delivery as a more sustainable freight solution. While the focus of this report is on cargo e-bike adoption, supportive infrastructure and policies would also benefit pedal-powered cargo bikes and other forms of micromobility, creating broader system benefits.

title: Social Gradients in Employment During and after the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: School of Economics and Business, NMBU, University of Oslo - Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research, University of Oslo - Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research, University of Oslo - Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research and University of Oslo - Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research

detail.title: Social Gradients in Employment During and after the COVID-19 Pandemic

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Research Council of Norway, grant numbers 315769, 316475, 341289.

publicationDetails.journalName: Skatteforsk Centre for Tax Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine employment effects of the COVID-19 crisis in Norway from March 2020 through June 2022: during the initial lockdown, through the subsequent recovery, and after the dust had settled. While we identify large and socially skewed effects of the crisis through its early phases, we find no long-term effects on employees exposed to early risk of job loss. For those employed at the onset of the pandemic, both the level and the socioeconomic composition of employment quickly returned to normal. In contrast, we find considerable negative long-term employment effects on people who were neither in employment nor in education when the crisis hit. We argue that these patterns can be explained by social insurance policies that gave priority to protecting existing jobs and to distribute benefits to those who were temporarily laid off. Given the extreme increase in the social insurance caseload, an almost unavoidable side effect was reduced capacity for providing services to the already non-employed.

title: Exchange Rate Regulations and Labour Market Performance: Evidence for Argentina
affiliations: Bournemouth University

detail.title: Exchange Rate Regulations and Labour Market Performance: Evidence for Argentina
detail.abstract: I study trends in real wages in Argentina for the 2002-2023 period using time series data sources. I estimate a dynamic wage equation to unpack the shortand long-run relationships during the period of exchange rate controls (2011-2015; 2019-2023). I find that in the long-run, exchange regulations reduce real wages by 9.1%. Interestingly, in the short-run, the effect is only significant through the fiscal policy, with a shift of-5.8%. Simulation results show that a stabilization program of the public expenditure in conjunction with the removal of regulations would improve real wages. The pace of recovery will ultimately depend on the credibility of the program, extent of labour market frictions (e.g. minimum wages, powerful trade unions) and the size of the informal economy.

title: Beyond Wealth: The N-CAPM and N-Black-Litterman
affiliations: Vietnamese German University

detail.title: Beyond Wealth: The N-CAPM and N-Black-Litterman
detail.abstract: We develop the N-CAPM, a general equilibrium model where investors value nonpecuniary attributes ("N-attributes") alongside wealth. Modeling preferences in a Hilbert space and solving under CARA and CRRA yields two priced directions: the market and a beta-neutral N-image. We prove the market portfolio is generically not mean-variance efficient. CAPM alpha decomposes into a systematic, omitted N-exposure and a residual, genuinely skill-based component. We derive the implied omitted-variable bias and introduce a double-neutralization operator that delivers unbiased tests and isolates skill. Under CRRA, the N-price co-moves with aggregate wealth. For practice, we provide an N-Black-Litterman prior and closed-form portfolio choice.

title: Tariffs, Trade Wars, and the Natural Rate of Interest
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

detail.title: Tariffs, Trade Wars, and the Natural Rate of Interest
detail.abstract:
What are the effects of tariff changes and trade conflicts on the natural rate of interest? This article investigates this question, using a multicountry, heterogeneous-agent trade model in which the natural rate of interest is determined by firms’ demand for capital and households’ supply of assets through their savings behavior. We analyze how the equilibrium interest rate evolves during the transition to higher unilateral tariffs and a global trade war. In the short run, tariffs reduce capital demand, and so the natural rate of interest must fall for households’ asset supply to line up with capital demand. In the long run, both asset supply and capital demand fall by similar amounts, which leads to little change in the long-run natural rate of interest.

title: Understanding Post-Growth in Business Organisations: Support, Predictors, and Systemic Challenges
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Psychological and Behavioural Science, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Understanding Post-Growth in Business Organisations: Support, Predictors, and Systemic Challenges
detail.abstract: Business organisations are major contributors to the climate crisis and therefore must play a central role in addressing it. Their ecological impact stems largely from being deeply embedded in an economic paradigm that prioritises continuous growth, despite increasing evidence that this model is incompatible with ecological sustainability. However, little is known about how professionals within these organisations perceive or support alternatives to this growth-oriented model. Our research addresses this gap by examining how business professionals perceive and support post-growth business practices, which seek to prioritise human well-being and ecological sustainability over the pursuit of continuous economic expansion. More specifically, we first assessed professionals’ endorsement of the postgrowth approach in business. Second, we examined their views on whether organisations should possess the capability, opportunity, and motivation needed to adopt post-growth practices, informed by the COM-B behaviour change model. Third, we investigated psychological and demographic predictors of their views. Finally, we examined perceived barriers to adoption. Surveying 409 UK business professionals, we found strong support for post-growth in business (86%). Nevertheless, participants underestimated peer support, revealing pluralistic ignorance. We also found that participants generally agree (61-89%) that organisations should have the capacity to adopt postgrowth business practices. The most consistent predictor of participants’ views was a desire to help address global challenges (i.e., transformative utopian impulse). Barriers included structural economic pressures and lack of training or awareness. These findings highlight both readiness for change and the systemic and perceptual obstacles that must be addressed to enable post-growth transformation within business organisations.

title: Profits and U.S. Tariff Policy Through a Kaleckian Lens: How Trump Built it, Biden Rewired it, and Trump Ii Scaled It
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Profits and U.S. Tariff Policy Through a Kaleckian Lens: How Trump Built it, Biden Rewired it, and Trump Ii Scaled It
detail.abstract: This article briefly reviews the recent evolution of U.S. tariff policy across three phases—Trump I, Biden, and Trump II—and interprets it through Michał Kalecki’s profits identity. National income accounting implies that, ceteris paribus, an improvement in the trade balance (X−M) raises aggregate domestic profits (P). Tariffs raise P by reducing imports (M) and, when they induce onshoring or friend‑shoring, by increasing investment. It is argued that this profit‑volume redistribution mechanismconverting foreign profits into domestic profits, which is largely neglected in mainstream trade discourse, is the common thread that transcends the disparate motives behind U.S. tariffs.

title: UNFRIENDING THE KIDS: The Problematic Race to Childproof Social Media

detail.title: UNFRIENDING THE KIDS: The Problematic Race to Childproof Social Media
detail.abstract:
A growing number of states have recently enacted new laws with the goal of protecting young people from harms allegedly caused by social media use.  These laws are diverse in their approaches but broadly seek to limit youth access to social media platforms by imposing age verification and parental consent requirements. These laws directly implicate the First Amendment rights of both young users who will no longer be able to access speech or speak on social media platforms as well as adult users who must now submit to age verification to access these quintessential forums for political discourse. 

These new social media age verification laws are just one part of a larger trend of new laws aimed at “childproofing” the internet.  Apart from social media, numerous states have recently enacted laws requiring pornographic websites to age authenticate users and to only allow users over the age of 18 to access pornographic material.  Parallel to these legislative developments, the Supreme Court’s June 2025 decision in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, has reshaped online age verification jurisprudence by upholding an online age verification law against a First Amendment challenge for the first time. 

This article contributes to the literature by first describing the many ways in which states are attempting to regulate youth social media usage.  It then examines the critical differences between pornographic websites and social media platforms.  Through examination of these differences, it becomes clear that the Court’s rationale in Free Speech Coalition is inapposite in the social media context.  Social media age verification statutes intrude on significantly more speech, including core political speech, and impose more burdensome restrictions on both adult and youth users than do laws governing access to pornographic websites.  Recognizing that statutorily age-gating social media platforms is problematic from both a constitutional and practical perspective, this article argues that policy makers would better serve the public by instead allocating resources for further research on the impacts of social media use on young users and by empowering youth social media users and their parents through education on the potential harms of youth social media use and the tools already available to parents to mitigate those harms.

reference: American Journal of International Law, forthcoming
title: Dystopian International Law
affiliations: University of Reading - School of Law

detail.title: Dystopian International Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Journal of International Law, forthcoming

detail.abstract:
In 2025, we international lawyers – and the legal system in which we operate – are standing at the precipice. That things are beyond bad should not be in doubt. This is not some run-of-the-mill crisis of the kind that international lawyers revel in, as Hilary Charlesworth warned us not to do. This is collapse, or something collapse-adjacent. And we are not alone, here at the precipice. Everyone else is here too. Some don’t think things are as catastrophic as they first seem. Some are delighted with how things are going (though there are few international lawyers among them). Some are despairing (and here the international lawyers are legion). Everyone’s anxious.

I, too, am anxious, standing here at the precipice. I see the looming catastrophe, for our world and for our field. The catastrophe is already here. It is in Gaza, in Sudan, in Ukraine. It is in the global decline of democracy and rising authoritarianism, including in the United States, the linchpin of the current international order. The question is how big this catastrophe is going to get, and what will come after it. And that we just don’t know. We can’t know, standing, as we are, here at the precipice.

In this essay, I would like to imagine, as an international lawyer, where the international legal system could go as we leave this precipice behind. The world we will live in in ten or twenty years’ time will in many ways be worse than when I write this. The international legal system will be worse with it. 

But dystopias are not inevitable. Where we go from this precipice, and just how bad things really end up being, is contingent. It depends on what we choose to do, or not do. Anyone who has lived through a dictatorship – and I have lived through three (kind of) – will know that the good guys don’t always win, but the bad guys don’t either. There are forks in the road, decisions and choices that people make. The decisions and choices of international lawyers are far from the most consequential, but they are ours.

I have chosen to engage with two books – both written by non-lawyers, for a general, mass market audience – as a starting point for discussing the precipice on which we stand. The first is a classic: Hannah Arendt’s The Origins of Totalitarianism, the first edition of which was published in 1951. The second is of more recent vintage: Anne Applebaum’s Autocracy, Inc., published in 2024.

Arendt’s work has provoked decades of scholarly commentary. She has also, for good reasons, experienced a surge in popularity in recent years, in response to the unravelling of democracy in a substantial number of states. Applebaum’s work is, of course, not canonical in the same way. But, despite their differences, and the seven decades’ gap between them, there are some important commonalities between these two books. Both resulted from an effort by scholars, who are not traditional academics but essayists writing books with a popular appeal, to make sense of the radical transformation of the world around them. Both books were written on a precipice. Both are intensely personal. And both have lessons to impart – for international lawyers and for all citizens – lessons that need to be absorbed.

title: Measuring FDI and Trade-related Interdependence Across Countries: The Case of the United States and China
affiliations: George Mason University - Schar School of Policy and Government, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) and Renmin University of China

detail.title: Measuring FDI and Trade-related Interdependence Across Countries: The Case of the United States and China
detail.abstract:
Based on the new integrated accounting framework of global supply chains (GSC) (Wang, Wei, Yu, and Zhu, 2025), we derive three types of economic dependence (producers’ dependence on upstream supplies, producers’ dependence on downstream markets, and consumers’ dependence on supply chains) that take into account of the presence of foreign invested firms as well as international trade. To measure indirect value flows between the origin and destination countries that are mediated through third economies, we show a need to go beyond both trade-in-value added and gross trade statistics. As an application, we derive new measures of inter-dependence between the United States and China.

title: Barriers to Foreign Aid Delivery in Conflict Zones: A Critical Literature Review
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: Barriers to Foreign Aid Delivery in Conflict Zones: A Critical Literature Review
detail.abstract: Foreign aid is critical for populations affected by armed conflict, yet its delivery is frequently obstructed by political agendas, security dynamics, and operational constraints. This literature review critically examines the mechanisms, motivations, and consequences of aid obstruction in conflict zones. The analysis identifies a range of actors such as state authorities, non-state armed groups, donor governments, and even aid organizations themselves, whose actions impede humanitarian access. Tactics include bureaucratic barriers, denial of movement, targeted violence against aid workers, and conditional aid tied to political objectives. Donor-driven strategies often prioritize foreign policy interests over humanitarian principles, while anti-terrorism laws further restrict operations. Internal shortcomings within the aid system, such as excessive security measures and inadequate local engagement, compound these challenges. The implications are profound: obstruction intensifies civilian suffering, undermines neutrality, fosters dependency, and can prolong conflict. The review emphasizes the need for adaptive, context-sensitive approaches that reinforce local participation, uphold humanitarian norms, and ensure accountability from both donors and operational agencies. Addressing these structural and political barriers is essential to safeguarding the integrity and effectiveness of humanitarian aid in the world's most volatile environments.

title: College Loans and Human Capital Investment
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Madison - Department of Economics, National Taiwan University - Department of Finance and University of Calgary - Department of Economics

detail.title: College Loans and Human Capital Investment
detail.abstract:
College loans serve as a double-edged sword for human capital investment: While they facilitate access to education, the burden of repayment may distort post-education investments in human capital. We examine the role of college loans and loan repayment policies through a structural model in which heterogeneous individuals, faced with borrowing limits, make dynamic decisions on consumption, borrowing/saving, labor supply, and costly human capital investment (via both college education and on-the-job learning a la Ben-Porath (1967)). We estimate two versions of the model using data from the NLSY79: one with natural borrowing limits and another with parameterized limits. Counterfactual simulations based on both models suggest that, relative to the standard fixed repayment plan, income-driven repayment (IDR) plans modestly increase educational attainment, lifetime earnings, and individual welfare. Although some generous IDR plans may result in losses for the loan program itself, overall government revenue is higher under IDRs than under the standard repayment plan when lifetime income taxes are accounted for, creating a win-win scenario for both individual welfare and government revenue.

title: Managing Waste or Wasting Management? A Critique of Republic Act 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
affiliations: and

detail.title: Managing Waste or Wasting Management? A Critique of Republic Act 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000

keywords: Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000

detail.abstract: This critique examines the implementation and effectiveness of Republic Act No. 9003, also known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, which was designed to address the Philippines' growing solid waste management challenges. The Act introduced an institutional framework through the National Solid Waste Management Commission (NSWMC) and mandated local government units (LGUs) to develop 10-year solid waste management plans focusing on waste reduction, recycling, and environmental sustainability. While RA 9003 has strengths such as its participatory approach, institutional depth, and potential for environmental and economic benefits, it suffers from critical weaknesses including inadequate funding, weak enforcement, limited infrastructure, and low public awareness. These challenges have hindered full compliance, as shown by the continued existence of open dumpsites and limited access to sanitary landfills and Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs). The critique recommends increased funding, stronger enforcement mechanisms, public-private partnerships, and comprehensive education campaign.

title: Gendered Impacts of Oil Price Shocks: Analyzing Women's Labor Force Participation in Petrostates

detail.title: Gendered Impacts of Oil Price Shocks: Analyzing Women's Labor Force Participation in Petrostates
detail.abstract: Oil wealth has been shown to negatively affect women's participation in the labor force. But does declining revenue from fossil fuels, due to the global energy transition, lead to higher female labor force participation (FLFP) and greater gender equality in petrostates? Such hypothetical/future-oriented questions are difficult to answer. This study gets around the challenge by conducting a mixed-method analysis to assess the relationship between oil price shocks and FLFP, emphasizing socioeconomic development and policy implications. Empirical findings indicate there is a causal link between oil price shocks and FLFP in petrostates, with falling oil prices associated with increases in participation and rising prices linked to declines. This relationship appears to be driven by female employment opportunities, government transfers and subsidies, foreign worker flows, and governance quality. Qualitative evidence from Saudi Arabia demonstrates how policy reforms following the 2014 oil price bust can increase FLFP. The results suggest that petrostates are likely to encourage greater women's labor force participation to maintain their prosperity amid diminishing oil revenues driven by the energy transition and global decarbonization efforts in the coming decades.

title: International Students, Immigration Policies and Implications for Innovation
affiliations: University of Massachusetts at Amherst - College of Social and Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics and Boston University School of Management

detail.title: International Students, Immigration Policies and Implications for Innovation
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the evolving trends and policy dynamics of international student migration, focusing on their implications for STEM workforce development and innovation. While the United States has remained a leading destination for international students, recent years have seen a plateau or decline in incoming students, contrasted by growth in countries like Canada, Australia, and emerging hubs such as China and India. International students, particularly in STEM fields, play a critical role in shaping host countries' innovation ecosystems, often transitioning to permanent residents and STEM workers. We review immigration policies, including post-graduation work and residency pathways, highlighting their varying impacts on student inflows and innovation. Policies in Canada and Australia have until recently eased these transitions, while restrictive measures in the U.S. and U.K. have posed challenges. By documenting these trends and policy shifts, we identify gaps in the literature and outline directions for future research at the intersection of international education, immigration, and innovation.

title: Job Mismatch and Early Career Success
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and Princeton University

detail.title: Job Mismatch and Early Career Success
detail.abstract:
How does being over- or underqualified at the beginning of a worker's career affect skill acquisition, retention, and promotion? Despite the importance of mismatch for the labor market, self-selection into jobs has made estimating these effects difficult. We overcome endogeneity concerns in the context of the US Air Force, which allocates new enlistees to over 130 different jobs based, in part, on test scores. Using these test scores, we create simulated job assignments based on factors outside of an individual's control: the available slots in upcoming training programs and the quality of other recruits entering at the same time. These factors create quasi-random variation in job assignment and hence how cognitively demanding an individual's job is relative to their own ability. We find that being overqualified for a job causes higher attrition, both during technical training and afterward when individuals are working in their assigned jobs. It also results in more behavioral problems, worse performance evaluations, and lower scores on general knowledge tests about the military taken by all workers. On the other hand, overqualification results in better performance relative to others in the same job: job-specific test scores rise both during technical training and while on the job, and these individuals are more likely to be promoted. Combined, these patterns suggest that overqualified individuals are less motivated, but still outperform others in their same job. Underqualification results in a polar opposite set of findings, suggesting these individuals are motivated to put forth more effort, but still struggle to compete when judged relative to others. Consistent with differential incentives, individuals who are overqualified are in jobs which are less valuable in terms of outside earnings potential, while the reverse is true for those who are underqualified.

title: A Comparative Legal Analysis of Revenue Distribution Between the States
affiliations: Alliance University

detail.title: A Comparative Legal Analysis of Revenue Distribution Between the States
detail.abstract:
The Goods and Services Tax that was introduced in India in 2017 actually went on to enable a revolutionary shift in the indirect taxation regime in the nation by consolidating a chain of state and central taxes into one system. GST is a seminal reform in the tax regime of India, altering the very essence of the Centre-State relationship. This single tax system is intended to abolish  cascading taxation effects, in addition to maintaining free flows of goods and services betweenstate boundaries. In this connection, determining who receives how much with the introduction of GST has been a topic of much discussion; queries have been raised regarding revenues shared between the Centre and the States. The legal framework of the GST is dealt with in the paper. It critically examines its implications for Indian federalism in light of comparable tax systems in the
 other federations, particularly in Australia and Canada. Performance and implications of revenue sharing devices towards financial autonomy of states in the Indian federal system are also examined.

The major problems that arise through this analysis are less fiscal independence of States primarily owing to centralizing the administration via GST and the postponement in the payment of compensation generating tensions in Centre-State relationships. This paper visualizes reforms in India's GST regime in the directions of more balanced centralization and State autonomy, guided by an international approach. Finally, while GST has established India's economic integration,
long-term success requires additional steps to address the issues of the State governments and strengthen cooperative federalism.

title: Fractured Sovereignty: OECD Pillar Rules and Canada's Constitutional and Compliance Challenges in Global Tax Reform
affiliations: Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE), University of Toronto

detail.title: Fractured Sovereignty: OECD Pillar Rules and Canada's Constitutional and Compliance Challenges in Global Tax Reform
detail.abstract: Canada’s dual-tax system and longstanding reliance on source-based principles place it in a uniquely precarious position under the OECD’s Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 frameworks. This paper offers a sovereignty-centered critique of the OECD’s evolving global tax order by analyzing the legal misalignments, enforcement burdens, and geopolitical ripple effects emerging from Canada's partial implementation of the two-pillar structure. Under Pillar 1, Canada’s decision to proceed with unilateral digital services taxation (DST), despite G7 pressure, has drawn direct retaliation threats from U.S. policymakers, including former President Donald Trump’s June 2025 campaign pronouncement to terminate bilateral tax negotiations. This reinforces that tax coordination is no longer technocratic—it is geopolitical. Under Pillar 2, Canada faces internal fragmentation. Federal authority to implement a global minimum tax sits uneasily with provincial autonomy over corporate income tax. Meanwhile, Canada’s longstanding FAPI regime, thin capitalization rules, and interest deductibility limits under sections 18.2 and 212.3 raise deep questions about how Pillar 2’s jurisdictional blending and GloBE top-up calculations will interact with pre-existing anti-deferral strategies. The paper argues that the OECD’s model glosses over such domestic legal pluralism, treating Canada as a unitary actor despite real administrative and political divergence. Without reconciling these internal and external sovereignty risks, Canada’s alignment with the two-pillar framework will remain partial, contentious, and potentially destabilizing.

title: Follow the carbon money: How capital market pricing of carbon risk shapes green transition of Chinese listed companies?
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: Follow the carbon money: How capital market pricing of carbon risk shapes green transition of Chinese listed companies?
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between corporate carbon risk exposure and green transition using a comprehensive sample of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2001 to 2023. We develop a new carbon risk exposure metric that circumvents reliance on corporate carbon emissions disclosures, thereby capturing both observable and latent carbon risks. Our analysis reveals a robust positive association between carbon risk exposure and subsequent green transition initiatives, suggesting that companies facing heightened carbon risk perceptions are more likely to adopt sustainability-oriented strategies. Mechanism analysis shows that financial constraints as a key mechanism driving this relationship. Companies with greater carbon risk exposure experience tighter financing conditions, which in turn motivates green transition efforts. Heterogeneity analysis further demonstrates that this effect is particularly salient for companies operating in regions with stronger environmental consciousness, where external pressures from local governments and the public amplify the linkage between carbon risk and green transition. Moreover, internal pressure arising from shareholders’ environmental concerns also accelerates the pace of corporate green transition. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the impacts of carbon risk and the drivers of green transition. Importantly, they highlight the role of financial markets as a catalyst for sustainable behavior of listed companies, particularly when investor perceptions of climate-related risks are factored into strategic decision-making processes.

title: The Hidden Costs of Subsidized Housing in Bogotá: Rent vs. Buy, Liquidity, and the False Promise of VIS/VIP
affiliations: Temple University - Mathematics Department

detail.title: The Hidden Costs of Subsidized Housing in Bogotá: Rent vs. Buy, Liquidity, and the False Promise of VIS/VIP
detail.abstract: We assemble a twenty-year rent-versus-buy framework for Colombia's VIS/VIP housing and include the frictions that most policy summaries omit: gray-delivery finishing financed at consumer rates, uncovered down payment financed at consumer rates, HOA and maintenance creep, CPI-indexed commuting time, transaction and illiquidity costs, and early-sale clawbacks. Under realistic CPI-linked rents and flat-to-negative real appreciation, we find no scenario in which VIS ownership beats renting within 20 years. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive financial analysis comparing total ownership costs to renting for Colombia's VIS program, despite widespread anecdotal evidence of quality issues and subsidy failures.

title: Monte Carlo Simulation - How to Simulate Asset Prices for Derivatives Pricing (Presentation Slides)
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School

detail.title: Monte Carlo Simulation - How to Simulate Asset Prices for Derivatives Pricing (Presentation Slides)
detail.abstract: This presentation provides a comprehensive introduction to Monte Carlo simulation for derivative pricing, with a focus on equity options. In Part 1, we review the theoretical foundations, covering stochastic asset price modelling using Geometric Brownian Motion, Ito’s Lemma, Girsanov’s Theorem, Change of Measure, Risk-Neutral Valuation, and the role of martingales and arbitrage in modern asset pricing theory. In Part 2, we apply these concepts in practice by implementing a Monte Carlo framework to price vanilla and exotic options. We first validate the methodology by benchmarking against closed-form Black–Scholes values for European options, before extending the framework to exotic derivatives and double barrier knock-out options. We further illustrate how simulations can be used to compute quantities such as exercise probabilities and knock-out probabilities, providing practical insights into structuring and optimizing exotic products in line with client-specific risk–return profiles.

title: Evaluating the Value of China’s South-South Cooperation in the Energy and Climate Space with a Focus on Decarbonization and Sustainable Development under Paris Agreement Commitments
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Evaluating the Value of China’s South-South Cooperation in the Energy and Climate Space with a Focus on Decarbonization and Sustainable Development under Paris Agreement Commitments
detail.abstract: China's South-South Cooperation (SSC) in energy and climate sectors plays a vital role in shaping global decarbonization efforts. This paper assesses the impact of Chinese overseas investments, especially in Indonesia and Africa, within the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and Paris Agreement commitments. Despite China's promise to peak carbon emissions before 2030 and reach net-zero by 2060, its substantial financing of coal-fired power plants and mineral extraction projects continues to tie developing countries to carbonintensive growth. Through case studies from Indonesia's coal and nickel industries and Africa's energy infrastructure, the research reveals the dual nature of China's role-supporting energy access on one hand, but also causing ecological damage, air and water pollution, displacement, and health risks on the other. The findings indicate that although China has begun investing in renewable projects like hydropower and solar energy, these efforts remain limited compared to fossil fuel investments. Ultimately, the paper argues that China's current investment approach undermines its SSC principles and Paris commitments, emphasizing the need for a fundamental shift toward sustainable financing and genuine renewable energy collaboration to meet global climate goals.

title: The Shape of U - On the Structure  of Utility \\ from Electric Vehicle Charging
affiliations: University of Cologne

detail.title: The Shape of U - On the Structure  of Utility \\ from Electric Vehicle Charging
detail.abstract: With the growing adoption of electric vehicles, understanding user charging behavior is increasingly important for informing operational, investment, and policy decisions regarding their integration into the power system.  While utility functions are commonly used to describe user preferences in charging behavior models, most existing studies rely on formulations with limited theoretical consistency and empirical validation, potentially leading to biased expectations. This paper empirically compares different utility function specifications and examines their implications for charging behavior modeling and charging station profitability. I introduce a novel discrete choice model framework to efficiently estimate utility function parameters from revealed preference data. Using a dataset of observed charging sessions at public charging stations in Germany, the model identifies accurate utility functions, uncovers charging preferences, and simulates station segment viability. The results suggest that charging utility is non-linear: marginal utility decreases with charged energy and marginal disutility increases with charging duration. An interaction between energy and duration leads to higher marginal valuation of energy for longer charging durations.  Stations profit from inelastic demand driven by users who highly value energy content, are less price sensitive, and engage in high-value activities at the charging location, such as in urban areas or traffic hubs.

reference: The Journal of African American History, volume 106, issue 4, 2021[10.1086/716492]
title: From Nkrumah's Black Star to the African Diaspora: Ghanaian Intellectual Activists and the Development of Black Studies in the Americas
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: From Nkrumah's Black Star to the African Diaspora: Ghanaian Intellectual Activists and the Development of Black Studies in the Americas

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Journal of African American History, volume 106, issue 4, 2021[10.1086/716492]

detail.abstract: After Kwame Nkrumah’s overthrow in 1966, a group of Ghanaian intellectuals brought their specific version of Pan-Africanism into the United States at precisely the moment when Black studies programs were being formed. Consequently, they shaped the trajectory of the field and linked it to a specifically African intellectual project. These Ghanaian intellectuals sought to inject an Africa-centered sense of what political education and political mobilization meant into the framework of Black studies. At the University of Massachusetts Amherst and Brown University, they worked to make Europe’s ongoing economic exploitation of Africa, the persistence of white supremacist regimes in southern Africa, and the US government’s support of these oppressive forces key parts of the otherwise US-centric curricula of Black studies programs. The role that Ghanaian intellectuals played in the United States helps us illuminate the unexplored intellectual impact of African scholars in the 1970s and 1980s outside of Africa on Black internationalism.

title: Modelling and analysis of multi-timescale uncertainty in energy system planning
affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) - Department of Industrial Economics and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

detail.title: Modelling and analysis of multi-timescale uncertainty in energy system planning
detail.abstract: Recent developments in decomposition methods for multi-stage stochastic programming with block separable recourse enable the solution to large-scale stochastic programs with multi-timescale uncertainty. Multi-timescale uncertainty is important in energy system planning problems. Therefore, the proposed algorithms were applied to energy system planning problems to demonstrate their performance. However, the impact of multi-timescale uncertainty on energy system planning is not sufficiently analysed. In this paper, we address this research gap by comprehensively modelling and analysing short-term and long-term uncertainty in energy system planning. We use the REORIENT model to conduct the analysis. We also propose a parallel stabilised Benders decomposition as an alternative solution method to existing methods. We analyse the multi-timescale uncertainty regarding stability, the value of the stochastic solution, the rolling horizon value of the stochastic solutions and the planning decisions. The results show that (1) including multi-timescale uncertainty yields an increase in the value of the stochastic solutions, (2) long-term uncertainty in the right-hand side parameters affects the solution structure more than cost coefficient uncertainty, (3) parallel stabilised Benders decomposition is up to 7.5 times faster than the serial version.

title: The Home Stretch: County-Level Policy Implementation and Regional Financial Development in China
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Economics, Fudan University - School of Economics, Fudan University and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Finance

detail.title: The Home Stretch: County-Level Policy Implementation and Regional Financial Development in China
detail.abstract: Hierarchical structures, where central authorities delegate powers to local governments, are ubiquitous but face implementation challenges resulting from weak accountability. This study presents one of the first evidence of how local officials’ policy implementation affects regional financial development in China—a deeply hierarchical polity with a historical struggle to bridge the “last mile” of policy execution. We develop a new index of county-level Central Financial Policy Implementation Index (CFPI) based on over 6.32 million news releases of county governments on their websites between 2009 and 2023. We find that stronger CFPI implementation is positively associated with local loan innovation, a proxy for financial development. We further document that these effects are more substantial for counties where the officials have a finance-related background and stronger promotion incentives. Our paper highlights the importance of addressing the “last mile” issue in policy implementation in a decentralized administrative system.

title: Sustainable Development Goals and Land Tenure Security in Uganda
affiliations: Makerere University

detail.title: Sustainable Development Goals and Land Tenure Security in Uganda
detail.abstract: Land tenure security is important for achieving a number Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The purpose of this paper was to investigate variation in land tenure security across three districts located in different geographical regions of Uganda. Using a quantitative cross-sectional survey data collected in early 2019. The findings show that Kanungu district found in SouthWestern Uganda had significantly higher levels of land tenure security as compared to Nakasongola (Central) and Nwoya (Northern). Research findings have implications on further study and benchmarking land governance systems in Kanungu. Furthermore, they have implications on implementation of government and donor land titling or registration programs in terms of priority areas. They further sheds light on the importance of accounting for geographical context in land tenure studies.

title: Public R&D Meets Economic Development: Embrapa and Brazil’s Agricultural Revolution
affiliations: , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Notre Dame University and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Public R&D Meets Economic Development: Embrapa and Brazil’s Agricultural Revolution
detail.abstract:
Can public R&D investment in developing countries drive productivity growth? We study this question in the context of Brazilian agriculture and the Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária (Embrapa), a public research corporation established in 1973 to develop locally suitable science and technology. First, we show that Embrapa redirected research toward prioritized staple crops and local ecological conditions, and increased research productivity, especially in remote and research-scarce regions. Second, exploiting the staggered rollout of research centers alongside heterogeneous local exposure to Embrapa’s technology development, we find that Embrapa significantly increased agricultural output, driven both by higher productivity and expanded input use. Combined with a model, these estimates imply that public R&D investment increased national agricultural productivity by 110% with a benefit-cost ratio of 17. The decentralized structure, in which research labs were spread across many ecological zones instead of in a single hub, explains a large share of these benefits.

title: Shield and Trap: Crop Insurance and the Adaptation Paradox
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington and Lincoln University

detail.title: Shield and Trap: Crop Insurance and the Adaptation Paradox
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the paradoxical role of crop insurance in shaping farmers’ responses to climate risk. Using a newly constructed county–crop–year panel dataset covering 1,686 U.S. counties from 1989 to 2023, we combine agricultural production data, PRISM climate records, EM-DAT disaster exposure, and USDA Risk Management Agency insurance data. We propose the concept of Insurance-Induced Adaptive Inertia (IAII) and formalize the Insurance Paradox Proposition: while crop insurance reduces short-run risk exposure through income stabilization, it simultaneously weakens long-run adaptive responses by locking farmers into maladaptive production structures.Empirically, our baseline fixed-effects models show that indemnity payments significantly stabilize crop shares, confirming the short-run buffering effect. However, the interaction of insurance variables with temperature and the IAII index reveals a systematic reduction in climate sensitivity, consistent with maladaptation. Robustness checks—including placebo tests, alternative insurance measures, and event-study designs—further support this finding. Moreover, policy heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that the 1994 Federal Crop Insurance Reform Act and the 2000 Agricultural Risk Protection Act amplified the paradox, as expanded subsidies deepened farmers’ adaptive inertia.Our results highlight an Insurance Paradox: crop insurance functions as both a shield and a trap—protecting farmers in the short run but eroding their long-run adaptive capacity. This challenges the conventional view that insurance unambiguously promotes adaptation and calls for policy designs that integrate resilience criteria into insurance programs.

title: Transdisciplinary Equilibrium (JX): in Dating Apps From Emotional Divergence to Recognition-Seeking Business / Anticipatory Suppression and Social Cost in Dating Platforms: A JX Framework Whitepaper
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Transdisciplinary Equilibrium (JX): in Dating Apps From Emotional Divergence to Recognition-Seeking Business / Anticipatory Suppression and Social Cost in Dating Platforms: A JX Framework Whitepaper
detail.abstract: This paper applies the Transdisciplinary Equilibrium (JX) framework to dating apps. Rather than neutral marketplaces for matching, platforms sustain recognition-seeking equilibria where emotional divergence (E), structural asymmetry (S), and anticipatory suppression (A) interact through a social cost function J(x) = αE(x) + βS(x) + γA(x) with α, β, γ ≥ 0 and α + β + γ = 1. We reconstruct common app experiences into schematic figures and dialogues (no screenshots), formalize threshold participation and interaction effects, and propose measurement, estimation, and design levers.

title: Open government data and corporate investment:Evidence from Chinese A-share Listed Companies
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Central University of Finance and Economics, Zhejiang University and Tianjin University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Open government data and corporate investment:Evidence from Chinese A-share Listed Companies
detail.abstract: The governmental governance environment significantly influences real corporate investment. Based on the data of listed A-share enterprises from 2010-2020,we adopt a heterogeneous timing difference-in-differences method to examine the impact of Open government data (OGD) on real corporate investment by leveraging the launch of OGD platforms. It is found that OGD significantly promotes real corporate investment. This conclusion remains robust after a series of tests for robustness and endogeneity, including parallel trend, placebo, heterogeneity treatment effect, and replacing variable. The analysis of the impact mechanism reveals that OGD influences real corporate investment by reducing enterprise uncertainty and alleviating financing constraint. The heterogeneity analysis indicates that OGD exerts a more pronounced investment promotion effect on non-state-owned enterprises, without political affiliations, regions characterized by intense government intervention, and areas exhibiting low social trust. This study contributes both conceptual insights for advancing the real economy with higher quality and practical recommendations to support the modernization of national governance structures and administrative effectiveness.

title: From the Arab Oil Embargo to Rare Earths: How Reactive Leadership Endangers U.S. National Security
affiliations: Emory University School of Law

detail.title: From the Arab Oil Embargo to Rare Earths: How Reactive Leadership Endangers U.S. National Security
detail.abstract: This paper examines the enduring consequences of reactive leadership on U.S. national security by drawing a parallel between the 1973 Arab oil embargo and the current crisis surrounding rare earth elements. Both episodes expose a dangerous pattern: the United States often fails to anticipate resource-based geopolitical threats until they escalate into full-blown crises. Despite the strategic warning embedded in the oil shock of the 1970s, the U.S. remains heavily dependent on foreign sources, now for rare earth minerals critical to advanced technologies and military systems. The paper argues that this failure to apply historical lessons has left national defense and technological capabilities vulnerable to external disruption, particularly from countries that dominate the global rare earth supply chain. Through historical analysis and contemporary policy critique, this work calls for a shift from reactive to proactive leadership grounded in strategic foresight. Securing access to critical resources must be treated not merely as an economic goal, but as a national security imperative.
