detail.abstract: We analyse the consequences of carbon price heterogeneity on households in The EU from 2010 to 2020. Accounting for both heterogeneity in carbon pricing across emission sources and the indirect effects from inter-industry linkages, we obtain two key findings. First, due to widespread carbon pricing exemptions, household burdens are lower than previously estimated. Second, lower-income groups are affected disproportionately, because they spend a smaller share of their expenditure on products that benefit from exemptions than their higher-income counterparts. Therefore, imposing uniform carbon prices both within and across countries would reduce carbon pricing regressivity on household expenditure in the EU. A global price would be most effective in this regard, as it would raise carbon prices embodied in EU imports. Further, because EU economies are open and apply higher average carbon prices than their trade partners, the domestic revenues exceed the costs embodied in EU household consumptions bundles. This increases the scope for reducing the burden of carbon pricing on lower-income households through revenue redistribution. Our results imply that the ongoing extension of carbon pricing to more sectors through the EU ETS II and the introduction of the EU's CBAM should make carbon pricing less regressive, all else equal.

title: A Web-Based Platform Bridging the Gap Between Contractors and Customers in the Construction Industry
affiliations: Bharati Vidyapeeth's College of Engineering and

detail.title: A Web-Based Platform Bridging the Gap Between Contractors and Customers in the Construction Industry
detail.abstract: The construction industry often grapples with issues related to trust, transparency, and accessibility-especially for individual customers and small contractors. Mirror Constr is a final year project designed to address these challenges through a digital platform that acts as a transparent mediator between customers and contractors. This research paper explores the platform's structure, features, and its potential to democratize the construction domain. By enabling contractors to showcase their work and ratings and allowing customers to float tenders, the platform brings balance and accessibility to an otherwise monopolized space. The study also focuses on how new civil engineers can benefit from easier market entry and more visibility. This paper presents an in-depth review of related works, discusses the relevance and scope of the study, outlines the research methodology, and concludes with findings that validate the platform's utility and innovation.

title: International Organizations as Actors in International Relations: Assessment of Effectiveness and Development Prospects
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: International Organizations as Actors in International Relations: Assessment of Effectiveness and Development Prospects
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the scope and prospects of international bodies with a particular focus on the role of the United Nations in contemporary global governance. With the ongoing rise of a multipolar world and the complex transnational issues of climate change, pandemics, and terrorism, the UN's traditional post-World War II configuration is increasingly under fire. This research addresses the urgent need reform the UN because of the of the surging perception that the UN is dysfunctional and its failure to cope with modern crises. 

This inquiry is approached through the three major theoretical paradigms of international relations: liberalism, neorealism, and constructivism. This paper uses these frameworks to explore the dominant challenges and opportunities for change of such institutional inertia. It discusses some specific changes such as the extension of the Security Council and the amendment of the General Assembly's voting procedures, stressing especially the absence of a decisive political will from the major powers. 

The findings reveal that for the United Nations to retain its relevance and functionality, the revamped structure must be underpinned by a significant change in the interplay of functionality and legitimacy. This is to emphasize that the reform of the UN must be approached in a balanced manner between the interests of the powerful states and the international community as a whole in order for the United Nations to provide an adequate response as a forum for the fundamental issues of the 21st century.

title: Applied Behavioral Tokenomics: A New Paradigm for Incentivized Human Action
affiliations: Independent, Independent and Independent

detail.title: Applied Behavioral Tokenomics: A New Paradigm for Incentivized Human Action
detail.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the term Applied Behavioral Tokenomics (ABT), coined in Saratoga, California, on August 24, 2025. We define ABT as the design and deployment of token-based systems that can directly shape, reinforce, and measure human behavior in applied social contexts. Unlike previous existing work on "behavioral tokenomics," which focuses on how consumers perceive token design in financial markets, ABT emphasizes real-world behavioral outcomes in major aspects of human life, such as education, rehabilitation, and workforce development. Built on behavioral economics pioneered by Nobel laureate Richard Thaler, ABT recognizes that individuals are influenced not only by external and internal rational incentives but also by heuristics, emotions, and social context. Through tokens embedded into structured reinforcement systems, ABT anchors behaviors to explicit sponsor-backed rewards or repellents, creating measurable and adaptive economies of action. The core principles of ABT include behavioral anchoring, positive and negative reinforcement, programmatic structuring of milestones or goals, sponsor-backed redemption economies, and continuous data feedback loops. Through this lifecycle, ABT proposes a paradigm in which societies incentivize action that is incentive-based rather than punitive and restorative rather than exploitative, while also being measurable. Our early applied model is EdKoin by EdKoin Educational Systems, Inc., a platform for tokenized behavioral reinforcement in schools, rehabilitation, and correctional systems, etc. EdKoin demonstrates how, through ABT, we aim to reduce recidivism risk and reinforce pro-social behavior.

title: Pension Reform and Stock Market Development
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Pension Reform and Stock Market Development
detail.abstract: It is widely believed that deep domestic stock markets must be in place before introducing funded pension schemes. However, this view creates a “chicken-and-egg” dilemma: policymakers prefer to launch pension reforms only when well-functioning stock markets exist, yet such markets often depend on the presence of long-term, rational institutional investors, such as private pension funds. In this paper, we show that one way to break this dilemma is to implement fully-funded, individually-owned, collectively-managed, mandatory/incentivized (FICMI) pension schemes. Our cross-country empirical analysis and a stylized model suggest that FICMI pension schemes can activate a virtuous cycle: the development of FICMI pension schemes can support domestic stock market growth, improve capital allocation, and foster economic growth. This, in turn, attracts institutional investors like pension funds, which further reinforce domestic stock market development. In addition, we highlight how FICMI schemes can address coordination failures and network externalities that deter long-term equity investment. We also discuss enabling conditions and policy design for successful implementation.

title: Earnings Instability
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago

detail.title: Earnings Instability
detail.abstract:
This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that the majority of U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. This earnings instability is pervasive, but it has been masked in past analysis of annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. This is because earnings instability arises in large part from firm-driven fluctuations in hours. This earnings instability is a meaningful source of economic risk: we provide causal evidence that it increases consumption volatility and also leads to greater job separations, and we find that workers have a high willingness to pay to reduce earnings instability. These findings suggest that short-term earnings risk is a significant and previously underappreciated feature of the labor market.

title: The Role of the Oil and Gas Sector in Shaping Trinidad and Tobago’s Economic Trajectory
affiliations: Fudan University

detail.title: The Role of the Oil and Gas Sector in Shaping Trinidad and Tobago’s Economic Trajectory
detail.abstract: The economy of Trinidad and Tobago has long been characterized by its reliance on the oil and gas sector, which has served as both the foundation of national prosperity and a source of structural vulnerability. This paper examines the central role of hydrocarbons in shaping the country's economic trajectory, highlighting how resource dependence has influenced patterns of growth, diversification, and long-term sustainability. Drawing on historical and contemporary data, the analysis situates Trinidad and Tobago within the broader framework of resource-based economies, engaging with theories of the "resource curse," Dutch disease, and economic rent distribution. The findings underscore the dual nature of the sector's impact. On one hand, oil and gas revenues have enabled Trinidad and Tobago to achieve relatively high levels of per capita income, finance extensive social programs, and maintain macroeconomic stability in comparison to many of its Caribbean neighbors. On the other hand, heavy dependence on hydrocarbons has hindered structural diversification, fostered exposure to volatile global energy markets, and created fiscal rigidities. These dynamics have contributed to cycles of boom and bust, with significant implications for employment, inequality, and public investment. The paper further considers the government's efforts to mitigate these challenges through policy interventions, such as the establishment of the Heritage and Stabilisation Fund, the promotion of downstream energy industries, and recent initiatives aimed at expanding non-energy sectors like tourism, financial services, and the creative industries. Despite these measures, the transition toward a more diversified and resilient economy remains incomplete, constrained by institutional, structural, and global market factors. Ultimately, the analysis demonstrates that while the oil and gas sector has defined the trajectory of Trinidad and Tobago's development, the sustainability of future growth depends on the country's capacity to leverage resource wealth into broader economic transformation.

title: Working Paper -Cognitive Fallow in AI Labour Markets: A Global Framework with an Australian Evidence Snapshot
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Working Paper -Cognitive Fallow in AI Labour Markets: A Global Framework with an Australian Evidence Snapshot
detail.abstract: This paper introduces cognitive fallow as a cohort-level condition in which highly educated new entrants experience prolonged, involuntary under-utilisation because artificial intelligence (AI) has automated or reallocated the entry-level cognitive tasks that historically served as stepping stones into professional work. We situate the concept within task-based technological change, graduate overeducation, and search-and-matching literatures; formalise a simple mechanism that predicts fewer junior vacancies and higher experience thresholds; and propose a Cognitive Fallow Index (CFI) built from graduate outcomes and vacancy data. Using a historical snapshot of the Australian labour market (July 2025), we calculate a national 'CFI-lite' proxy to test for aggregate-level distress. The resulting null signal at this aggregate level demonstrates the masking effect of broad occupational categories and motivates the paper's primary contribution: a framework for granular, field-specific measurement required to detect hidden entry-level bottlenecks. We outline an identification strategy (event study and triple differences) and a policy programme-targeted hiring credits, apprenticeship-style AI fellowships, and skills-linked procurement-grounded in matching externalities and human-capital depreciation. The framework turns diffuse "AI job loss" debates into measurable, testable bottlenecks at labour-market entry and provides an evaluation-ready agenda for policymakers.

title: The Algorithm Advantage: Ranked Application Systems Outperform Decentralized and Common Applications in Boston and Beyond
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Algorithm Advantage: Ranked Application Systems Outperform Decentralized and Common Applications in Boston and Beyond
detail.abstract:
School choice systems increasingly use common applications, where students can apply to multiple schools on a single form, though schools make admission decisions independently. We model three application systems: a common application, a decentralized system with costly separate applications, and a ranked-choice system using a matching algorithm. Our model shows that while a common application may expand access, it increases competition and may produce worse matches than a decentralized system where application costs encourage more selective applications. Ranked-choice systems combine reduced application costs with preference-based matching that reduce mismatches. We examine these predictions by analyzing how Boston's charter school sector was affected when it adopted an online common application. Counterfactual simulations suggest the common application performs no better than alternatives on several metrics and did little to increase access for disadvantaged groups. A ranked system consistently outperforms a common application across various levels of competition and assumptions on preference stability between application and enrollment stages.

title: The Tax Redistribution Gap

detail.title: The Tax Redistribution Gap
detail.abstract: The tax revenue gap-the difference between how much the IRS collects in tax revenue and how much it should collect based on the text of the Internal Revenue Codeis both well-defined and well-studied. But raising revenue is just one purpose of taxation; the tax code also operates to redistribute wealth. Drawing from the tax revenue gap and redistribution literatures, this article coins a parallel concept, the tax redistribution gap, to map the extent to which the tax system falls short of its redistributive goals. Introducing a tax redistribution gap measure challenges background assumptions in current tax discourse: first, it would call out a reliance on pre-market income as a distributive baseline, which serves to overstate the redistributive impact of the tax code; second, it would increase the profile of redistribution among policymakers and the publicunderstandably, measures like the tax revenue gap and tax expenditure budgets focus dialogue on tax evasion and over-spending by the government. Ultimately, the tax redistribution gap would provide a single measure that displays how we are falling short of a key task of the state (redistribution). And by understanding and comparing the component ways our current tax systems falls short of it intended outcomes, we can better tailor redistributive policy solutions.

title: When Westphalia Goes to (Greater) China: Territory, Sovereignty and legal Narratives Across the Strait
affiliations: Amsterdam Center for International Law

detail.title: When Westphalia Goes to (Greater) China: Territory, Sovereignty and legal Narratives Across the Strait

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Territorial and Maritime Studies / Volume 5, Number 1 / Winter/Spring 2018 / pp. 23–41

detail.abstract:
The present study aims to reconceptualize the underlying tenets of Westphalian links between sovereignty and territoriality, showing how an "exported" eurocentric doctrine actually functions in a distinct legal environment-post-imperial China-and the manner in which a protracted political-ontological dispute can or cannot make use of established Western-based legal mechanisms. 

Approach-By focusing on the cross-strait dilemma of overlapping claims to sovereignty upon a "greater" China-advanced both by the People's Republic of China and the Republic of China (Taiwan)-we aim to show how volatile (and fragile) the functionality of Westphalia actually is. In this regard, we first concentrate upon the "genealogy" of Westphalia itself, as well as on the competing narrative of Sinocentric regional order, setting the scene for an unavoidable clash of paradigms. Afterwards, it is shown how the allegedly victorious vision of Westphalia was rewritten (and conceptually undermined) when applied to the cross-strait divergence. 

Findings-By following a genealogical path of Westphalia and of the intra-Sinic dispute, the present enquiry shows that a eurocentric concept (such as sovereignty) is ill-suited to address challenges that occur in such different legal-political frameworks. Moreover, it can be discerned that even though Westphalia could have been of some (albeit limited) use when european and non-european actors collided, it is unable to deliver a path forward for polities that were both part of a common non–Westphalian system.

Originality—When taken apart, neither the analysis of Westphalia, nor of the Sinocentric paradigm structurally reconfigure the shape of the present debates. However, it is a leap forward to join them together into a larger narrative about crosscultural collisions, showing how even a neutralized Westphalia is dysfunctional in polities with a distinct (and strong) political tradition.

title: Characterizing Optimality in Dynamic Settings: A Monotonicity-based Approach
affiliations: Harvard University, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Characterizing Optimality in Dynamic Settings: A Monotonicity-based Approach
detail.abstract:
We develop a novel analytical method for studying optimal paths in dynamic optimization problems under general monotonicity conditions. The method centers on a locator function—a simple object constructed directly from the model’s primitives—whose roots identify interior steady states and whose slope determines their local stability. Under strict concavity of the payoff function, the locator function also characterizes basins of attraction, yielding a complete description of qualitative dynamics. Without concavity, it can still deliver sharp results: if the function is single crossing from above, its root identifies a globally stable steady state; if the locator function is inverted-U-shaped with two interior roots (a typical case), only the higher root can be a locally stable interior steady state. The locator function further enables comparative statics of steady states with respect to parameters through direct analysis of its derivatives. These results are obtained without solving the full dynamic program. We illustrate the approach using a generalized neoclassical growth model, a rational (un)fitness model, and a learning-by-doing economy.

detail.abstract: As far back as Independence, agriculture has contributed a significant amount to the development of the economy. During the financial year 1950-1951, agriculture accounted for 59% of the country's total GDP. While the agriculture sector has been declining, (17.8% of the GDP for the year 2019-20), it still plays an important role in the Indian economy and 54.6% of the total workforce is engaged in agricultural and allied sector activities (Census 2011) and accounts for Given the importance of the agriculture sector, the Government of India has taken several steps for its development in a sustainable manner. Steps have been taken to improve the income of farmers. The present paper seeks to understand paddy crop production elasticity and returns to scale in the Warangal District in Telangana State. Paddy crop is grown both in the kharif and rabi seasons in the country. As for the agricultural ministry's advanced estimates for the Kharif session of 2022-23, India's Paddy production is likely to decline by 6% to 104.99 million tonnes in the Kharif session. Paddy cultivation in Telangana hit a new high this Yasangi crop season with the crop sown in nearly 54 lakh acres, a staggering increase of 160 percent when compared to the season's normal cultivation area of 33.53 lakh acres. Paddy was cultivated on 64.54 lakh acres during Vaanakalam (Kharif) season of 2022-23 and 35.84 lakh acres during the Yasangi season of 2021-22.

title: Artificial Writing and Automated Detection
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Artificial Writing and Automated Detection
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used for written deliverables. This has created demand for distinguishing human-generated text from AI-generated text at scale, e.g., ensuring assignments were completed by students, product reviews written by actual customers, etc. A decision-maker aiming to implement a detector in practice must consider two key statistics: the False Negative Rate (FNR), which corresponds to the proportion of AI-generated text that is falsely classified as human, and the False Positive Rate (FPR), which corresponds to the proportion of human-written text that is falsely classified as AI-generated. We evaluate three leading commercial detectors—Pangram, OriginalityAI, GPTZero—and an open-source one —RoBERTa—on their performance in minimizing these statistics using a large corpus spanning genres, lengths, and models. Commercial detectors outperform open-source, with Pangram achieving near-zero FNR and FPR rates that remain robust across models, threshold rules, ultra-short passages, "stubs" (≤ 50 words) and ’humanizer’ tools. A decision-maker may weight one type of error (Type I vs. Type II) as more important than the other. To account for such a preference, we introduce a framework where the decision-maker sets a policy cap—a detector-independent metric reflecting tolerance for false positives or negatives. We show that Pangram is the only tool to satisfy a strict cap (FPR ≤ 0.005) without sacrificing accuracy. This framework is especially relevant given the uncertainty surrounding how AI may be used at different stages of writing, where certain uses may be encouraged (e.g., grammar correction) but may be difficult to separate from other uses.

title: A Chip Off the Old Block? Genetics and the Intergenerational Transmission of Socioeconomic Status
affiliations: , University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Southern California - Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR), USC Center for Economic and Social Research and

detail.title: A Chip Off the Old Block? Genetics and the Intergenerational Transmission of Socioeconomic Status
detail.abstract: Progress in understanding the role of genetics in intergenerational socioeconomic persistence has been hampered by challenges of measurement and identification. We examine how the genetics of one generation influences the SES of the next by linking genetic data from the Dutch Lifelines Cohort to tax records for 2006-2022. Our genetic measure is the polygenic index (PGI) for educational attainment. To isolate causal genetic effects, we exploit randomness in genetic transmission across generations. One generation’s genetics impacts the education, income, and wealth of the next. A 10-percentile increase in one generation’s PGI raises next generation’s education by 0.11 years. “Next-generation genetic effects” are also large relative to “same-generation genetic effects”: a 10-percentile increase in a person’s PGI raises their income by 0.9 percentiles and their child’s by 0.7 percentiles, indicating strong persistence across generations. We next turn to mechanisms: about half of next-generation genetic effects reflect direct genetic inheritance (“genetic transmission”). The remainder operates through environmental pathways (“genetic nurture”): one generation’s genetics shapes the circumstances in which the next is raised. This environmental channel is reinforced by assortative mating: high-PGI individuals select more-educated, higher-earning partners. Our findings underscore that genetics is one of the forces anchoring SES across generations.
